answer:
FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, natural language):

"Among NLSY79 respondents observed in 1989 (ages 24–32), the likelihood of having withdrawn more money from savings than put in declines with age. In the raw data the rate falls from 25.1% at ages 24–26 to 20.6% at ages 30–32. In the primary logistic model (DISSAVED on AGE, AGE_2, log(1+INCOME), GENDER, BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC; HC1 robust SEs), the age profile is mildly concave — the probability of dissaving peaks around age 25 and then declines steadily, from about 0.253 at age 24 to about 0.184 at age 32 (≈ −0.9 percentage points per year on average; the AGE and AGE_2 terms are jointly significant, Wald p < 0.001; the quadratic turning point of the fitted logit is age ≈ 25.1). The gradient strengthens markedly when respondents whose savings did not change or who had no savings (SAMESAVE=1) are excluded — predicted dissaving falls from 0.42 at age 24 to 0.26 at age 32 (−16.7 pp; AGE p=0.007, AGE_2 p=0.003) — indicating that part of the measured age decline in the all-inclusive definition comes from older respondents being more likely to be active net savers rather than simply less likely to draw down. A linear-in-age logit gives the same qualitative answer (−0.047 log-odds per year, p < 0.001). Within this narrow 24–32 window, dissaving is most likely in the mid-20s and becomes progressively less likely toward age 32.

Caveats (required and observed): This is a single cohort (NLSY79) observed at a single point in time (1989) over a narrow age range (24–32), so age cannot be separated from cohort or calendar-year effects and no causal claim is warranted. The age gradient is sensitive to the mean-imputed rows: when the ~4,300 rows with income imputed to the sample mean (47.279) and/or BMI imputed to its mean (25.159) are excluded (n=8,430) or flagged with imputation dummies, the quadratic age terms lose significance and the fitted age profile is essentially flat (0.283–0.293); the honest reading is a real, statistically robust decline with age in the raw and SAMESAVE-excluded data whose size, though not its direction, is imputation-sensitive. Additional limitations: DISSAVED=0 pools net savers with no-change/no-savings respondents (the literal variable definition, per the approved primary specification), income is right-skewed with a top-code at 1,057.448 and 131 zeros, 12 BMI values exceed 60 (dropping them does not change the age result), no survey weights or respondent IDs are available, and the data show 2,151 exact duplicate rows consistent with the imputation process."

KEY EVIDENCE (all from the executed script outputs/analysis_nls_bmi.py):
- PRIMARY (all-inclusive, n=12,686): AGE +0.4354 (SE 0.2432, p=0.073), AGE_2 −0.0087 (SE 0.0044, p=0.047); centered-age refit gives the identical profile with the linear term now precise (−0.0510, SE 0.0096, p<0.001 — pure AGE/AGE_2 collinearity, VIF≈688, not an estimation problem); joint Wald p<0.001; pseudo-R²=0.0061.
- Predicted P(dissaved), covariates at means: 24→0.2529, 25→0.2548 (peak), 26→0.2533, 28→0.2408, 30→0.2167, 32→0.1837; average marginal effect −0.0086/yr.
- Age-bin rates with CIs: 24–26 = 25.1% [23.7, 26.4] (n=4,138); 27–29 = 24.5% [23.3, 25.7] (n=4,831); 30–32 = 20.6% [19.3, 21.9] (n=3,717).
- SECONDARY (SAMESAVE=1 excluded, n=7,901): AGE +0.7424 (SE 0.2761, p=0.007), AGE_2 −0.0149 (SE 0.0050, p=0.003); predicted P: 24→0.4240 … 32→0.2572; raw subsample rates 45.1% (24) → 25.0% (32). The two specifications agree on direction and concavity; the secondary one is steeper — the disagreement is in magnitude, reported as such.
- Robustness: excluding mean-imputed INCOME/BMI rows (n=8,430): AGE terms p≈0.56, profile flat (0.285→0.283); primary + imputation flags: age terms p≈0.45, flags themselves strongly significant (BMI_IMPUTED −2.01, p<0.001) — imputed rows behave very differently, confirming sensitivity; linear-in-age: AGE −0.0467 (SE 0.0092, p<0.001); dropping BMI>60 (n=12,674): virtually identical to primary (AGE +0.4361, AGE_2 −0.0087).
- Covariate notes (secondary to the age question): higher income and FEMALE and BLACK are associated with higher dissaving in the primary model (LINC +0.119, FEMALE +0.200, BLACK +0.205, all p<0.001; HISPANIC +0.100, p=0.093; BMI not significant, p=0.27). The INCOME sign flips in the imputed-excluded sample (+0.31), another symptom of imputation sensitivity.

MODEL CHOICES APPLIED (per approval): all-inclusive specification is primary; SAMESAVE-excluded is the key secondary result; log(1+INCOME); HC1 robust SEs; imputation-flag model added beyond the agreed list as a cheaper way to show the same sensitivity the exclusion test shows.

EXECUTED WORKFLOW: inspect → descriptive rates by age/gender/race/income-quartile/BMI-quartile → primary logit with quadratic age → marginal-effect age profile and turning point → Wilson-CI age-bin rates → SAMESAVE-excluded logit → imputed-row-exclusion logit → linear-in-age logit → BMI>60-exclusion logit → imputation-flag logit → joint Wald tests, centered-age stability check, VIF diagnostics → model-comparison and age-profile CSVs. No results were fabricated; all numbers above come from the printed model output.

payload.hypothesis: Among NLSY79 respondents aged 24-32 in 1989, the likelihood of withdrawing more from savings than putting in declines with age: raw rates fall from 25.1% (ages 24-26) to 20.6% (ages 30-32); the primary logit (AGE, AGE_2, log(1+INCOME), GENDER, BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC; HC1 SEs) yields a concave profile peaking near age 25 and falling from ~0.253 at age 24 to ~0.184 at age 32 (~-0.9 pp/yr; joint Wald p<0.001). Excluding SAMESAVE=1 respondents sharpens the decline (0.42 to 0.26). The gradient is directionally robust but magnitude-sensitive to mean-imputed INCOME/BMI rows. Single cohort, one year, ages 24-32 only: no causal or life-cycle claim is supportable.
payload.workflow: Inspection (missingness, coding, DISSAVED x SAMESAVE cross-tab) -> descriptive age-bin rates with Wilson CIs -> primary logit of DISSAVED on AGE, AGE_2, log(1+INCOME), FEMALE, BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC with HC1 robust SEs -> predicted-probability age profile, marginal effects, turning point -> robustness: SAMESAVE-excluded logit, mean-imputed-row exclusion, imputation flags, linear-in-age logit, BMI>60 exclusion -> joint Wald tests, centered-age stability check, VIF diagnostics -> model-comparison table -> natural-language hypothesis.
limitations: Single cohort (NLSY79), single year (1989), ages 24-32 only: age not separable from cohort/year effects; no causal claim
Age gradient loses significance when mean-imputed INCOME/BMI rows are excluded or flagged: magnitude is imputation-sensitive
